The Grey-breasted mountain toucan (Andigena hypoglauca) is a striking ramphastid inhabiting montane cloud forests of the northern Andes. Field studies of its reproductive biology indicate that eggs are incubated at a relatively low temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], and hatching occurs after an incubation period of 17 days [ab = 17 days]. This developmental duration is comparable to that of other mid-sized Andean toucans, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a high-altitude environment where thermal stability within the nest cavity is critical for successful embryogenesis. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a modest body mass of 18 grams [Ww0 = 18 grams], a low value that places the neonate at a distinct disadvantage in a cool environment, requiring intensive brooding by both parents to maintain optimal body temperature during the first days of life. The initial investment in small hatchlings may be offset by a rapid growth trajectory, given the need to reach fledging mass before the onset of the wet season reduces foraging efficiency. Parents coordinate feeding and brooding duties with remarkable synchrony, a pattern common among cloud-forest ramphastids that face unpredictable fruit availability.

As the nestling period progresses, the developing chick undergoes a swift phase of mass increase. Under the thermal conditions typical of this species, which correspond to a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] during active metabolic periods, the time from hatching to fledging is approximately 41 days after hatching [tx = approximately 41 days after hatching]. This relatively brief nestling phase, in comparison to some lowland congeners, may be an adaptation to the shorter breeding season characteristic of high-elevation environments where fruit phenology imposes a narrow window for successful reproduction. During this period, the chick progresses through distinct developmental stages, from an altricial, down-covered nestling dependent on parental provisioning to a fully feathered individual capable of sustained flight. The fledgling then enters a post-fledging dependency phase during which it learns to forage independently while still receiving supplemental food from its parents. This transition is energetically demanding, and the young bird must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to buffer against periods of food scarcity during its first months of independent life.

Sexual maturation in Andigena hypoglauca occurs relatively early compared to other ramphastids of similar body mass. Field observations suggest that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the development of adult plumage, is attained at approximately 123 days after hatching [tp = approximately 123 days after hatching] when birds are maintained at their typical active body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This timing allows young individuals to reach reproductive condition within their first year, an adaptive trait for a species that faces high adult mortality from predation and harsh montane weather. The first successful breeding event, however, is typically deferred until the second year of life, with the time since birth at first brood estimated at roughly 1.9 years since birth [tR = roughly 1.9 years since birth] under optimal thermal conditions at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This delay reflects the substantial energetic investment required to attain full adult body mass and to develop the foraging skills necessary to provision a clutch successfully. During this pre-reproductive period, subadult birds often join mixed-species foraging flocks, where they refine their fruit-handling techniques and learn to exploit the patchy distribution of key food plants.

Adult body mass in this species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a lower ultimate wet weight compared to males. Maximum recorded body mass for adult females reaches 290.75 grams [Wwi = 290.75 grams], whereas adult males are substantially heavier, with an ultimate wet weight of 338.75 grams [Wwi = 338.75 grams]. This degree of dimorphism is typical of ramphastids, where males often engage in aggressive contests over nest cavities and foraging territories. The mass difference also has implications for reproductive energetics, as the smaller female invests considerable resources in egg production, typically laying two to three eggs per clutch. The maximum reproductive rate, inferred from the congener Ramphastos dicolorus, suggests that under favorable conditions this species can produce approximately 7 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 7 clutches annually] when maintained at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], though in wild populations the actual frequency is likely lower due to limitations in nest site availability and food abundance. Lifetime reproductive output is therefore constrained by both the relatively small clutch size and the extended interval between successful nesting attempts.

Respirometry trials conducted on captive individuals at a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C] have provided key insights into the species' metabolic physiology. The maximum basal metabolic rate was measured at 310.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 310.91 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the elevated energy demands associated with maintaining homeothermy in a cool montane habitat at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This metabolic rate is consistent with predictions for a bird of this body mass based on allometric scaling relationships, though it sits at the higher end of the range for ramphastids, likely due to the thermoregulatory costs imposed by the species' high-elevation distribution. Longevity records from banding studies indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 15.6 years [am = approximately 15.6 years] when birds are active at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], though captive individuals have been documented to persist for slightly longer under protected conditions. The combination of early maturation and relatively high reproductive output, balanced against an extended adult lifespan, suggests that Andigena hypoglauca occupies an intermediate position along the slow-fast life-history continuum, a pattern that may be shaped by the stochastic and seasonal nature of its cloud-forest environment.
